title: Groundwater doctrine and the limits of hydrological mapping
bodyMd:
For most of the nineteenth century, common-law courts treated groundwater as a legal mystery. Surface streams could be seen, measured, and divided; what moved beneath a landowner's field was, in the phrase of one early opinion, secret and occult. Courts responded with the rule of absolute ownership: a landowner could pump without limit, and a neighbour whose well went dry had no remedy. The rule was not a judgment about hydrology so much as a confession of ignorance about it.

Two doctrines later displaced it. The reasonable-use rule permits unlimited pumping so long as the water is applied to a beneficial purpose on the overlying land; it restrains only waste and export. The correlative-rights rule goes further, treating all overlying owners as sharers in a common supply and proportioning withdrawals when the aquifer cannot satisfy everyone. Both doctrines were framed as corrections of the older rule's indifference to neighbours, and both were made possible by the emergence of a science capable of mapping what courts had called occult.

That science, however, has proved a less obliging ally than the doctrines assume. Each rule presupposes that an aquifer's boundaries can be drawn, so that the set of owners entitled to share is determinable. Modern hydrology describes instead a continuum: aquifers leak into one another across semipermeable layers, and many exchange water with the very surface streams that the law allocates under an entirely separate body of rules. A pump three miles from a river may deplete it after a delay of decades. The legal categories require edges; the physical system supplies gradients.

Some commentators conclude that groundwater doctrine should therefore be abandoned in favour of administrative permitting, in which a regulator allocates withdrawals according to modelled effects rather than ownership of the overlying surface. The proposal is attractive, but it should not be mistaken for an escape from the difficulty. A permitting regime must still decide whose interests count and over what horizon, and the models on which it relies carry uncertainties that widen precisely as the time scale lengthens. What changes is not the indeterminacy but the institution that absorbs it: from a court deciding between two parties to an agency deciding for a basin.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage about water law. It describes the nineteenth-century rule of absolute ownership of groundwater, the reasonable-use and correlative-rights doctrines that replaced it, a conflict between those doctrines' assumption that aquifers have determinable boundaries and modern hydrology's picture of aquifers as a continuum, and the author's reservations about replacing the doctrines with administrative permitting. There are no figures, tables or mathematical notation.

provenance.notes: Written from scratch for this item bank. Not adapted from, and not a paraphrase of, any LSAC passage or any published article. The legal doctrines named (absolute ownership, reasonable use, correlative rights) are general textbook categories of water law; the argument, structure and wording are the author's own. The quoted phrase 'secret and occult' is attributed vaguely to 'one early opinion' as a period-flavour device and is not presented as a citable quotation.
